Madrid. The capital and largest city of Spain, located in the heart of the Iberian Peninsula at the geographical center of the country.

Geographically centered on the Iberian Peninsula, Madrid's strategic location contributed to its selection as Spain's capital by Philip II in fifteen sixty-one. The city rose to prominence during Spain's Golden Age in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries when the Spanish Empire was at its height. The Alcázar Palace served as the royal residence during this period.

Madrid became the center of Spanish artistic and intellectual life. Miguel de Cervantes spent his final years there, and Don Quixote achieved its greatest success in Madrid. The city is home to the Prado Museum, one of Europe's finest art repositories, founded in eighteen nineteen. It contains masterworks by Velázquez, Goya, Bosch, and other Spanish and European painters. The Prado holds works by Velázquez including Las Meninas, Goya, and El Bosco, and is one of Europe's finest repositories reflecting Spain's imperial cultural legacy.

During the Spanish Civil War from nineteen thirty-six to nineteen thirty-nine, Madrid endured a brutal three-year siege. The city's suffering became a symbol of the conflict and inspired artistic responses. The Alcázar Palace, residence of Spanish monarchs for centuries, was destroyed during the Civil War, and the Royal Palace now serves as the official royal residence.

Modern Madrid is Spain's largest metropolitan area and economic center. The city hosts European Union institutions and remains culturally dominant within Spain. Madrid's Retiro Park, established in the seventeenth century as royal grounds, is now a major public space exemplifying the city's transformation from monarchy-centered to democratic urban center.

The Madrid metro system is one of Europe's largest and most efficient, constructed largely in the twentieth century and essential to modern urban life. Modern Madrid balances its role as Spain's political capital with Barcelona's cultural rivalry, and regional tensions between Madrid-centered Spanish nationalism and Catalan independence reflect broader Spanish divisions.
